Yes. **`mbx setup` should get users all the way to working Cargo commands inside Codex.** Currently it installs the shim, then leaves users to fix PATH themselves. Worse, `setup --status` can report success when the shim exists but Cargo still bypasses it.

I’d aim for this new flow:

```sh
mbx setup --codex
```

It would:

- Configure persistent activation for Codex, preserving existing settings.
- Use the stable shim so mbx upgrades don’t break it.
- Check that ordinary `cargo` actually resolves through mbx in a fresh shell.
- Check access to the shared cache.
- Support matching `--status` and `--uninstall` operations.

The tricky part is persistent activation. Codex supports explicit shell environment settings, but we should avoid freezing the user’s current PATH into its config. Its worktree setup scripts are intended for provisioning; they aren’t documented as a persistent PATH mechanism. [Configuration reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference), [local environments](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/environments/local-environment).

**My first priority would be automatic shell activation plus honest verification**, with a Codex-specific entry point that handles the details. That would remove the current “installed successfully, silently unused” failure mode. A fresh Codex worktree running plain `cargo check` should be the acceptance test.

This is a proposed interface; I haven’t changed the code yet.
but what would it do

Mostly, it would **put mbx’s Cargo shim on the PATH that Codex’s shell commands use**. There’s no special Codex cache integration required.

For macOS/zsh, a concrete implementation would:

1. Install the existing stable Cargo shim.
2. Add a marked, removable block to the appropriate shell startup file that prepends the shim directory to PATH.
3. Start a fresh shell and verify that `cargo` resolves to that shim.
4. Tell you to start a new Codex session so it picks up the change.

Then Codex runs `cargo test` normally, and mbx handles caching and build coordination automatically across worktrees.

That does affect other shells too. A Codex-only alternative is setting PATH in Codex’s config, but that risks capturing a PATH that becomes stale.

So my earlier `--codex` suggestion was premature. **The useful feature is `mbx setup` offering to configure shell activation automatically**, then verifying it actually works. A dedicated Codex flag only makes sense if we establish a reliable Codex-only activation mechanism.

We’d need to:

**There’s no existing rustup wrapper setting, but there’s a clean feature we could propose.** I checked your installed rustup 1.29.1, its current settings, and proxy dispatch code.

The existing options help only partly:

| Option | Usefulness for mbx |
|---|---|
| `rustup which cargo` | Finds the selected toolchain’s actual Cargo executable—useful for avoiding recursion. |
| `rustup run <toolchain> …` | Runs mbx with a particular toolchain’s environment, but requires explicit invocation. |
| `rustup toolchain link` | Could register a custom toolchain containing our wrapper, but projects selecting stable/nightly would bypass it. |
| Disable automatic self-update | Doesn’t establish ownership of the Cargo proxy; it isn’t a durable integration mechanism. |

Custom toolchains select an entire toolchain; they don’t add a wrapper around whichever toolchain a project chooses. [Toolchains](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/concepts/toolchains.html), [selection rules](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/overrides.html).

I’d propose **a user-level Cargo wrapper setting in rustup**, with illustrative syntax:

```sh
rustup set cargo-wrapper /absolute/path/to/mbx
```

Then:

```text
cargo +nightly build
  → rustup selects nightly
  → mbx /path/to/nightly/bin/cargo build
  → actual Cargo
```

Rustup already selects the toolchain before constructing the command, so that provides a natural place to insert the wrapper. mbx would need to support that explicit-executable calling convention. [Proxy implementation](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustup/blob/main/src/cli/proxy_mode.rs).

The proposal should specify:

- Persistent user configuration that survives rustup updates.
- The resolved Cargo executable passed directly to the wrapper.
- Toolchain environment preserved.
- Defined recursion protection and a bypass mechanism.
- No change to project toolchain selection.

That would work for Codex, editors, and terminals whenever they invoke rustup’s Cargo proxy.

**There’s also an existing Cargo proposal: [#8188, “Support for cargo wrapper”](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/8188).** Putting the feature in Cargo itself would additionally cover installations that don’t use rustup. I’d reference that discussion when proposing the rustup approach—the key question is which project should own the integration.
